name: Amazon MWAA
oneLiner: Managed Apache Airflow for authoring and scheduling data pipelines.
whatItIs: MWAA is AWS's managed Apache Airflow. Airflow is the de-facto open-source tool for orchestrating data pipelines: you define workflows as DAGs (directed acyclic graphs) in Python, and Airflow schedules them, runs the tasks in order, handles retries and dependencies, and shows it all in a web UI. MWAA runs and scales the Airflow environment (scheduler, workers, web server, metadata DB) for you, so you get standard Airflow without operating the infrastructure. It's the coordinator that says 'run the ingest, then the transform, then load the warehouse' across your other AWS services.

inPractice.narrative: A nightly pipeline must run in order: pull data to S3, run a Glue ETL job, then trigger a Redshift load, and alert on failure. An engineer writes an Airflow DAG in Python with those tasks and dependencies; MWAA schedules it, runs each step via AWS operators, retries failures and surfaces the run in the Airflow UI. MWAA doesn't move the data itself — it conducts the other services in the right order at the right time.

coreConcepts.detail: Workflows are Python-defined directed acyclic graphs of tasks with dependencies. Code-as-config makes pipelines versionable, testable and dynamic.
Tasks use operators (e.g. GlueJobOperator, RedshiftSQLOperator, S3 sensors) from Airflow provider packages to talk to AWS and external systems.
Airflow's components: the scheduler triggers DAGs, workers execute tasks, the web server serves the UI. MWAA provisions and autoscales these.
You upload DAG files, plugins and requirements to an S3 bucket; MWAA syncs them into the environment — that's how you deploy pipelines.
You pick an environment class (small/medium/large) and MWAA autoscales workers between min/max to match task load.
Built-in retry policies, backfilling of past runs, and sensors that wait for external conditions make robust scheduling straightforward.

whenToUse: Orchestrating multi-step data pipelines across AWS services in a set order.
Teams already using or wanting standard open-source Airflow, managed.
Complex dependencies, retries, backfills and scheduling as code.
Coordinating Glue, EMR, Redshift, Lambda and external systems from one place.
Portability of DAGs to/from self-managed Airflow.
whenNotToUse: Simple event-driven, serverless step sequencing — AWS Step Functions is lighter.
A single trigger-one-function job — a Lambda + EventBridge schedule suffices.
Real-time/streaming data flow — Airflow orchestrates batch, it isn't a stream processor.
Tiny workloads where an always-on Airflow environment isn't cost-justified.

source.quote: Use Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow, a managed service for Apache Airflow, to set up and run data pipelines in the cloud at scale. … With Amazon MWAA, you can use Apache Airflow and Python to create workflows without managing infrastructure.

keyFacts.label: Role
keyFacts.value: Batch pipeline scheduling and dependency orchestration.

source.quote: Automatic scaling – Automatically scale Apache Airflow workers (the compute resources that run your tasks) by setting minimum and maximum limits.

keyFacts.label: Integrations
keyFacts.value: Airflow AWS provider operators + community providers.

source.quote: Amazon MWAA supports open-source integrations with Amazon Athena, AWS Batch, Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon DynamoDB, AWS DataSync, Amazon EMR … as well as hundreds of built-in and community-created operators and sensors.

pricingShape: MWAA bills for the environment being up: an hourly charge by environment size, plus additional worker/scheduler compute as it autoscales, plus a little storage for the metadata DB. Because Airflow's scheduler runs continuously, there's a baseline cost even when no DAGs are executing — an idle environment isn't free, unlike per-invocation services. So MWAA is economical when you have steady orchestration needs; for occasional or purely event-driven flows, Step Functions' pay-per-transition model is often cheaper.
gotchas: The environment runs 24/7, so it bills even when no DAGs run — not ideal for tiny/occasional use.
Python dependency management (requirements.txt/plugins) is a common source of environment breakage — pin versions.
Airflow orchestrates but doesn't process data; heavy compute belongs in Glue/EMR, not in a task.
Upgrading Airflow versions can break DAGs/providers — test in a non-prod environment.
Scheduler/worker sizing matters: too small and DAGs queue and lag their schedules.
